sources.SENG: sengpielaudio, 'Absorption coefficients of building materials and finishes' (compiled 125-4000 Hz table; original lab/method not stated per row) - https://sengpielaudio.com/calculator-RT60Coeff.htm
sources.SHARP: Sharp, B.H. (1978) 'Prediction methods for the sound transmission of building elements', Noise Control Eng. 11:53-63; field-incidence form R = 20log(m f) - 47 as restated by Tadeu & Mateus - https://baes.uc.pt/bitstream/10316/4037/1/filee0aec1aa21024e55b37c28755f99fb89.pdf ; Sharp model validated vs measurements in Mansilla et al. (IOA) - https://www.ioa.org.uk/system/files/publications/J%20MANSILLA%20F%20MASSON%20I%20CALDER%C3%93N%20DE%20PALMA%20L%20PEPINO%20L%20BENDER%20SOUND%20INSULATION%20OF%20HOMOGENOUS%20SINGLE%20PANELS%20A%20COMPARISON%20BETWEEN%20REAL%20CONSTRUCTION%20MATERIALS.pdf
sources.MIKI: Miki, Y. (1990) 'Acoustical properties of porous materials - modifications of Delany-Bazley models', J. Acoust. Soc. Jpn (E) 11(1):19-24; Delany & Bazley (1970) Applied Acoustics 3:105-116 (equations recalled from the papers, not re-fetched)
sources.EMBL: Embleton, Piercy & Daigle (1983) 'Effective flow resistivity of ground surfaces determined by acoustical measurements', JASA 74:1239, doi:10.1121/1.390029 - abstract confirms new snow 10-30, grass 150-300, asphalt ~30000 kPa s/m2; other rows (dirt, forest floor, sugar snow) recalled, not re-verified
sources.LAYER: Normal-incidence transmission through a homogeneous layer between two identical fluids: tau = |cos(kd) + (i/2)(Z2/Z1 + Z1/Z2) sin(kd)|^-2 (standard result, e.g. Kinsler et al., Fundamentals of Acoustics); complex k and Z from loss factor
sources.LOSSF: Building-material loss factors: brick 0.01-0.02, dense concrete ~0.02, oak ~0.01, fir ~0.008, glass 0.0006-0.002, cork 0.13-0.17 - scribd 'Damping Properties of Materials' (attribution unclear; consistent with Cremer, Heckl & Petersson, Structure-Borne Sound) - https://www.scribd.com/doc/239287321/Damping-Properties-of-Materials
sources.COMSOL: COMSOL blog 'Damping in Structural Dynamics: Theory and Sources' (concrete 0.02-0.05, steel 1e-4-1e-2, rubber 0.05-2) - https://www.comsol.com/blogs/damping-in-structural-dynamics-theory-and-sources
sources.VIB: Principles of Vibration (2nd ed.), Appendix C: steel 5-8e-4, aluminium 2-3e-4, concrete 2-3e-2, wood 2-4e-3, soft rubber 3-5e-2 - https://www.globalspec.com/reference/74164/203279/appendix-c-assorted-material-constants
sources.OLY: Olympus/Evident NDT 'Material sound velocities' (copper 4660 m/s, steel 1020 5890 m/s, cast iron 3500-5600 m/s) - https://www.olympus-ims.com/en/ndt-tutorials/thickness-gage/appendices-velocities/ (values seen via search snippet; page fetch was not completed)
sources.KD: Karl Deutsch 'Basic knowledge about ultrasonic testing' velocity table (window glass 5770 m/s, 2.51 g/cm3; quartz crystal 5760 m/s, 2.65 g/cm3) - https://www.karldeutsch.de/ndt-knowledge/basic-knowledge/basic-knowledge-about-ultrasonic-testing/?lang=en
sources.CLASS: CLASS Ltd sound velocity table (ice ~4000 m/s) - https://www.classltd.com/?p=5191
sources.HONEY: Rufo et al. (2021) Sensors 21(20):6748 - ultrasonic pulse velocity in honey 2125 m/s (25-45 C) - https://mdpi.com/1424-8220/21/20/6748
sources.GEL: Gelatin sound speed 1520-1650 m/s, attenuation 0.12-1.5 dB/cm/MHz - J. Mater. Sci.: Mater. Med. (2026) - https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10856-026-07020-7
sources.SANDV: Shallow dry sand P-wave 87-390 m/s (KFUPM dune study) - https://pure.kfupm.edu.sa/en/publications/p-wave-velocity-at-shallow-depths-in-sand-dunes-and-its-effect-on/ ; surface alluvium 180-255 m/s (Steeples et al., GRL 26(2):279) - https://kuscholarworks.ku.edu/bitstream/1808/17259/1/SteeplesD_GRL_26(2)279.pdf
sources.MOSS: TU Delft, 'Evaluating mosses on bioreceptive concrete' (impedance tube; peak 0.86, mean up to 0.48 over 50-6400 Hz) - https://repository.tudelft.nl/record/uuid:f5734366-f4e2-494f-969e-6bc7042a2879 ; LBTU 2026 (Pleurozium schreberi peak 0.62) - https://erdev.lbtu.lv/sites/default/files/proceedings/2026/TF090.pdf
sources.STRAW: Mas & Everbach (ASA 130th mtg, 1995): stuccoed 20-inch straw-bale wall TL 59.8 dB(A) - https://acoustics.org/pressroom/httpdocs/130th/lay03.html ; bale walls Rw 44-52 dB and straw impedance-tube data: D'Alessandro, Schiavoni & Bianchi, 'Straw as an acoustic material' (IOA) - https://www.ioa.org.uk/system/files/publications/F%20D%27ALESSANDRO%20S%20SCHIAVONI%20F%20BIANCHI%20STRAW%20AS%20AN%20ACOUSTIC%20MATERIAL.pdf
sources.ISO9613: ISO 9613-2:1996 Annex A Table A.1, attenuation through dense foliage (dB/m for 20-200 m paths). Values RECALLED, not re-verified online (standard is paywalled); method confirmed by Arup Strutt help - https://strutt.arup.com/help/Environmental_Noise/EnviroFoliageAtten.htm
sources.AINSLIE: Ainslie & McColm (1998) 'A simplified formula for viscous and chemical absorption in sea water', JASA 103(3):1671, doi:10.1121/1.421258 (formula as implemented in echopype - https://echopype.readthedocs.io/en/v0.9.1/api/echopype.utils.uwa.calc_absorption.html)
sources.MARCZAK: Marczak (1997) JASA 102:2776 - pure-water sound speed polynomial (recalled); Mackenzie (1981) JASA 70:807 nine-term seawater equation (recalled)
sources.KIEFFER: Kieffer (1977) 'Sound speed in liquid-gas mixtures: water-air and water-steam', JGR 82:2895 - small gas fractions lower mixture sound speed by up to ~3 orders of magnitude - https://www.eri.u-tokyo.ac.jp/people/ichihara/vp2007plan/Kieffer1977jgr.pdf
sources.MELT: Silicate-melt acoustics: Ai & Lange (2008) JGR doi:10.1029/2007JB005010; Rivers & Carmichael (1987) JGR 'Ultrasonic studies of silicate melts'. Numeric values for basaltic melt NOT retrieved this session; lava values below are estimates
sources.ODEON: Scattering: ISO 17497-1:2004 definition; Odeon practice of a single mid-band (500/1000 Hz) value expanded to other bands - https://odeon.dk/pdf/in05_1782.pdf ; typical range <0.05 (gypsum board) to >0.5 (audiences) - https://www.tvtechnology.com/opinions/coefficients-for-acoustical-materials
sources.BARK: UCL (2020) 'Sound absorption by tree bark' (context only; per-band values not extracted) - https://discovery-pp.ucl.ac.uk/10094490/1/Sound%20absorption%20by%20tree%20bark2020.pdf
sources.SNOW: Snow impedance-tube studies: Zhou et al. 2012 (WSL/Fraunhofer, 125-1600 Hz, porosity 46-90%) - https://publica.fraunhofer.de/handle/publica/228468 ; Hokkaido 1965 snow impedance - https://eprints.lib.hokudai.ac.jp/repo/huscap/all/20232/A20_p23-63.pdf
sources.MCWIKI: Minecraft Wiki - Wool (occludes_vibration_signals) and Carpet (dampens vibrations) - https://minecraft.fandom.com/wiki/Wool
sources.TEXT: General textbook values (Kuttruff 'Room Acoustics'; Bies & Hansen 'Engineering Noise Control'; Cremer/Heckl 'Structure-Borne Sound'; USDA Wood Handbook; rock-physics tables) - RECALLED, not re-verified online this session

dense_stone.absNote: Estimated between measured 'marble/tile' and 'brick, unglazed' rows (SENG) - natural cut stone, neither polished nor jointed.
dense_stone.note: Granite/limestone-like rock. c and rho from rock-physics tables (granite 2600-2700 kg/m3, Vp 4500-6000 m/s). Rock eta ~ 1/Q with Q 100-300 -> 0.003-0.01.

polished_stone.note: Marble/quartzite-like polished stone; also quartz blocks and smooth stone.

cobblestone.absNote: Estimated from 'brick, unglazed' (SENG) plus a little for open mortar joints; no measured rubble-masonry row found.
cobblestone.note: Rubble masonry: lower bulk density and stiffness than solid rock because of mortar and voids. Strong surface relief -> high scattering.

stone_bricks.absNote: Measured row 'Brick: unglazed' (SENG) used as surrogate for dressed stone masonry.

sandstone.absNote: Estimated: porous unsealed sedimentary stone, slightly above unglazed brick. No measured row found.
sandstone.note: Sandstone 2000-2400 kg/m3, Vp 2000-3500 m/s. Also used for tuff, coral blocks, sulfur blocks and coal block (see mapping notes).

brick.note: Fired clay brick 1800-2000 kg/m3; eta 0.01-0.02 (LOSSF). Also nether bricks (invented, fired-brick analogue) and mud bricks/packed mud (adobe, lighter in reality).

concrete.note: Dense poured concrete. Published eta ranges 0.005-0.05; 0.01 is the common building-acoustics assumption (Gilford & Gibbs, IOA).

terracotta.absNote: Estimated between 'brick, unglazed' and 'marble/tile' (glazed ceramic) rows (SENG).
terracotta.note: Fired clay without joints. Glazed terracotta is closer to the tile row (0.01-0.02).

packed_earth.note: Dirt/grass ground. Effective flow resistivity 400 kPa s/m2 sits between grass (150-300, EMBL) and roadside dirt (300-800, recalled). Frame P-wave ~300 m/s from shallow-soil seismic data (SANDV). Soil damping ratio 2-5% -> eta ~0.1.

mud.absNote: Estimated: saturated mud surface is acoustically hard, like the measured water row (SENG) slightly roughened.
mud.note: Water-saturated silty clay treated as a fluid (marine-sediment-like: 1500-1800 kg/m3, ~1500 m/s; Hamilton-type sediment attenuation ~0.1-0.5 dB/m/kHz -> eta ~0.02). Recalled values.

sand.note: Dry loose sand. Flow resistivity 300 kPa s/m2 is an estimate (fine sands are typically 100-1000+). Frame speed 250 m/s within measured 87-390 m/s for shallow dune sand (SANDV). Also used for concrete powder.

gravel.note: Loose clean gravel has large open pores, so its flow resistivity is much lower than sand's. 30 kPa s/m2 is an estimate (railway-ballast-like). No direct measurement found this session.

snow.note: Settled/packed snow ~300 kg/m3; porosity = 1 - 300/917. Flow resistivity above new snow (10-30, EMBL) toward 'sugar snow' (25-50, recalled). Frame speed estimated.

powder_snow.note: Fresh powder ~50-100 kg/m3; flow resistivity in the new-snow range 10-30 kPa s/m2 (EMBL). Frame speed estimated.

ice.note: Polycrystalline ice ~3800-4000 m/s (CLASS lists 4000). eta of ice near 0 C is estimated (internal friction 1e-3 to 1e-2).

glass.absNote: Measured row 'Glass: 1/4 in plate, large' (SENG). The 125 Hz value is panel resonance of a mounted pane: right for windows/panes, too high for a solid glass cube.
glass.note: Window glass 2500 kg/m3, cL 5770 m/s (KD); eta 0.0006-0.002 (LOSSF). Gameplay TL is based on the thin-pane figure, because Minecraft glass blocks play the role of windows.

obsidian.absNote: Surface treated as 'Marble/Tile' (SENG) - smooth glassy surface.
obsidian.note: Real volcanic glass (2350-2600 kg/m3). Its sound speed is estimated from silicate glasses (window glass 5770 m/s, KD); no obsidian-specific measurement found.

wood_planks.absNote: Measured row 'wood on joists' (SENG); low-frequency bump is panel resonance, a deliberate choice so plank rooms sound 'warm'.
wood_planks.note: Softwood/oak average 450-750 kg/m3; c is along-grain (3500-5000 m/s); across grain is ~1/3 of that. eta: oak ~0.01, fir ~0.008 (LOSSF). Wood is strongly anisotropic, so treat the thin (door) TL as indicative.

logs.absNote: Estimated for bark-covered solid timber; bark absorption studied in BARK but per-band numbers were not extracted.
logs.note: Solid (green or seasoned) timber with bark. Also bamboo blocks and nether stems/hyphae (fungal, invented -> wood analogue).

leaves.absNote: Estimated. Foliage mainly scatters; absorption rises with frequency as leaves vibrate and air flows through gaps.
leaves.note: Dense foliage is mostly air: sound passes through gaps. TL is the ISO 9613-2 per-metre foliage attenuation (recalled values). Density is foliage biomass per unit volume (estimate). Also used for plants, flowers, crops, vines and cobwebs.

wool.note: Felted wool block. Flow resistivity 25 kPa s/m2 (estimate; wool insulation is typically 5-30, rising with density). Absorption is derived and checks against measured 50 mm fibreglass/foam rows (SENG). Frame is limp (estimated frame speed 20 m/s, eta 0.3). Gameplay figure is deliberately boosted above stone to match sculk vibration occlusion.

carpet.absNote: Measured row 'carpet on foam' (SENG); Minecraft carpet is ~6 cm thick, so the thick-carpet row fits better than 'carpet on concrete'.
carpet.note: Same bulk as wool. Thin TL is what matters (carpets are 1/16 block).

hay.note: Straw/hay bale 80-150 kg/m3. Flow resistivity estimated (loose straw is low, single-digit kPa s/m2). Cross-check: real bale walls reach Rw 44-52 dB only with plaster (STRAW). Bare 1 m of hay is lower at low frequency. Also dried kelp, target, straw bed.

sponge.note: Analogue: open-cell polyurethane foam (25-35 kg/m3, ~5-20 kPa s/m2). Derived absorption checks against measured PU foam rows (SENG). Real sea sponge is a similar open-cell structure.

wet_sponge.analogue: Water-saturated open-cell foam, which acoustically is close to a water layer with a lossy frame. No direct measurement found.
wet_sponge.absNote: Estimated: water-filled pores make the surface nearly as hard as water.
wet_sponge.note: Also used for water-rich plant flesh (melon, pumpkin, cactus): rho ~950-1000, c ~1400-1500.

moss.note: Thick moss/peat mat. Flow resistivity from the forest-floor range (20-80, recalled from EMBL). Derived absorption agrees with impedance-tube peaks of 0.6-0.86 (MOSS). Also mushroom blocks, wart blocks, shroomlight (soft organic, invented).

iron.absNote: Estimated: thick smooth metal behaves like marble/tile. (Thin sheet metal on a frame absorbs more at low frequency.)
iron.note: Steel 1020: 5890 m/s (OLY); eta 5-8e-4 (VIB). Iron bars/chains/rails are mostly open space: the mod should scale by collision fill.

copper.note: Copper 4660 m/s (OLY). eta ~0.002 recalled from Cremer/Heckl table (TEXT). Copper grates are perforated: scale TL by open area.

gold.note: Gold 19300 kg/m3, longitudinal ~3240 m/s (TEXT, recalled). eta estimated. Also bells.

netherite.analogue: Tungsten heavy alloy (~17000-18500 kg/m3, tungsten Vp ~5200 m/s): netherite is described as gold alloyed with an ultra-dense, blast-proof material.
netherite.note: Also ancient debris and heavy core.

crystal.note: Amethyst = quartz: 2650 kg/m3, 5760 m/s (KD). Quartz Q ~1e4-1e6 (recalled) gives an extremely low loss factor, so it rings, which suits amethyst chimes. Diamond/emerald blocks are mapped here as 'gemstone'. Real diamond would be ~18000 m/s and 3515 kg/m3.

bookshelf.absNote: Estimated: irregular book spines and paper edges absorb and scatter moderately. No measured row found.
bookshelf.note: Wood frame plus stacked paper; bulk values estimated (paper 700-1150 kg/m3 with air gaps). Also TNT (paper + sand casing, invented).

slime.analogue: Gelatin/hydrogel (1520-1650 m/s; 0.12-1.5 dB/cm/MHz). Elastic gel matches the in-game bounce, so damping is low.
slime.absNote: Estimated: water-like impedance, so the surface is very reflective.
slime.note: eta derived from 0.5 dB/cm/MHz extrapolated linearly to 1 kHz (eta = 2*alpha*c/omega ~0.003). Shear damping of gels at audio frequencies is much higher (0.1-0.3, estimate). Also frogspawn and froglights.

honey.absNote: Estimated: liquid surface, like the water row (SENG).
honey.note: Honey 1420 kg/m3, 2125 m/s (HONEY). Viscous loss eta = (4/3)mu*omega/(rho c^2) with mu ~10 Pa s: ~1e-5 at 1 kHz, rising with frequency. Rounded up to 1e-4 to stay conservative. Honey block only.

wax_resin.absNote: Estimated: smooth, hard-ish polymer surface, slightly softer than glazed tile.
wax_resin.note: Solid wax and hardened resin. Beeswax ~960 kg/m3, plant resin/amber ~1050-1100 kg/m3 (recalled). Sound speed and damping are estimated from amorphous polymers (rubber-to-plastic range, eta 0.02-0.1). Covers honeycomb block, candles and resin blocks/bricks/clumps.

water.note: Fresh water at 10 C (Marczak). See media section for seawater and absorption with distance.

lava.absNote: Estimated: crusted, rough molten-rock surface; hard but irregular.
lava.note: Bubble-free basaltic melt: rho 2600-2750 and c ~2300-2900 m/s (estimate; literature values not retrieved). eta is the viscous figure (mu ~100 Pa s). Real lava with a few % gas can drop to <100 m/s (KIEFFER; see media section).

netherrack.analogue: Scoria / vesicular volcanic rock: netherrack is soft, crumbly, reddish and found by lava, which fits a porous, lightweight volcanic rock with higher internal damping.
netherrack.absNote: Estimated: open vesicles absorb a little more than dense masonry, much less than the open-textured 'concrete block coarse' row (SENG).

end_stone.analogue: Porous limestone / chalky stone: pale, pitted and lighter-looking than overworld stone.
end_stone.note: Also purpur and end portal frame (invented).

soul_sand.analogue: Loose silty, organic-rich sand: slows entities, so a looser and more damped granular bed than sand.

sculk.analogue: Soft, hydrated biological tissue (rho ~1050, c ~1540 m/s, the standard soft-tissue value) with a velvety fibrous surface. Damping is set high because sculk 'absorbs' vibrations in lore.
sculk.absNote: Invented: a fuzzy organic mat over tissue, rising with frequency like a thin fibrous layer.
sculk.note: All sculk blocks, sensors, shrieker and catalyst.
